<|channel|>analysis<|message|>We need to analyze the judgment text and not mention which of the options is not mentioned. The question:

"According to the judgment, when the court analyzed the reasons why PepsiCo’s advertisement did not constitute a unilateral offer in the form of a reward, which of the following reasons was not mentioned?"

Let's parse the options:

A. A reward advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the obligations mentioned in the advertisement.

B. As long as someone fulfills the content specified in the reward advertisement, the advertiser must fulfill their obligation.

C. A reasonable and objective person would not consider PepsiCo's advertisement to be an offer.

D. Reward advertisements that ask people to take specific actions are generally based on non-commercial reasons.

We need to look at the judgment section where the judge considered the rationale regarding "Reward" acts.

We will look at relevant section in the holding. Let's locate the section. Indeed, it appears: "III. Discussion" maybe. The relevant part named "2. Rewards as Offers" is part in the judgement. Let's read it.

Under "II. Discussion" - section B. "Defendant's Advertisement Was Not An Offer". Then sub-head "2. Rewards as Offers". The judge references case law: Carbolic Smoke Ball, Hell etc. The court discusses that.

Below, list bullet points? Let's examine.

I'll write out relevant portion:

```
2. Rewards as Offers

In opposing the present motion, plaintiff largely relies on a different species of unilateral offer, involving public offers of a reward for performance of a specified act. Because these cases generally involve public declarations regarding the efficacy or trustworthiness of specific products, one court has aptly characterized these authorities as "prove me wrong" cases. See Rosenthal v. Al Packer Ford, 36 Md.App. 349, 374 A.2d 377, 380 (1977). The most venerable of these precedents is the case of Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., 1 Q.B. 256 (Court of Appeal, 1892), a quote from which heads plaintiff's memorandum of law: "[I]f a person chooses to make extravagant promises ... he probably does so because it pays him to make them, and, if he has made them, the extravagance of the promises is no reason in law why he should not be bound by them." Carbolic Smoke Ball, 1 Q.B. at 268 (Bowen, L.J.).

Long a staple of law school curricula, Carbolic Smoke Ball owes its fame not merely to "the comic and slightly mysterious object involved," A.W. Brian Simpson. Quackery and Contract Law: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Company (1893), in Leading Cases in the Common Law 259, 281 (1995), but also to its role in developing the law of unilateral offers. The case arose during the London influenza epidemic of the 1890s. Among other advertisements of the time, for Clarke's World Famous Blood Mixture, Towle's Pennyroyal and Steel Pills for Females, Sequah's Prairie Flower, and Epp's Glycerine Jube-Jubes, see Simpson, supra, at 267, appeared solicitations for the Carbolic Smoke Ball. The specific advertisement that Mrs. Carlill saw, and relied upon, read as follows: “100 £ reward will be paid by ... ” etc.

...

Like Carbolic Smoke Ball, the decisions relied upon by plaintiff involve offers of reward. In Barnes v. Treece, 15 Wash. App. 437, 549 P.2d 1152 (1976), for example, the vice-president of a punchboard distributor, in the course of hearings before the Washington State Gambling Commission, asserted that, “I'll put a hundred thousand dollars to anyone to find a crooked board. If they find it, I'll pay it.” Id. at 1154. Plaintiff, a former bartender, heard of the offer and located two crooked punchboards. Defendant, after reiterating that the offer was serious, providing plaintiff with a receipt for the punchboard on company stationery, and assuring plaintiff that the reward was being held in escrow, nevertheless repudiated the offer. Id. at 1154. The court ruled that the offer was valid and that plaintiff was entitled to his reward. Id. at 1155.

Other "reward" cases underscore the distinction between typical advertisements, in which the alleged offer is merely an invitation to negotiate for purchase of commercial goods, and promises of reward, in which the alleged offer is intended to induce a potential offeree to perform a specific action, often for noncommercial reasons. In Newman v. Schiff, 778 F.2d 460 (8th Cir.1985), for example, the Fifth Circuit held that a tax protestor's assertion that, "If anybody calls this show ... and cites any section of the code that says an individual is required to file a tax return, I'll pay them $100,000," would have been an enforceable offer had the plaintiff called the television show to claim the reward while the tax protestor was appearing. Id. at 466-67. The court noted that, like Carbolic Smoke Ball, the case "concerns a special type of offer: an offer for a reward." Id. at 465. James v. Turilli, 473 S.W.2d 757 (Mo.Ct.App.1971), arose from a boast by defendant that the "notorious Missouri desperado" Jesse James had not been killed in 1882, as portrayed in song and legend, but had lived under the alias "J. Frank Dalton" at the "Jesse James Museum" operated by none other than defendant. Defendant offered $10,000 "to anyone who could prove me wrong." Id. at 758-59. The widow of the outlaw's son demonstrated, at trial, that the outlaw had in fact been killed in 1882. On appeal, the court held that defendant should be liable to pay the amount offered. Id. at 762; see also Mears v. Nationwide Mutual Ins. Co., 91 F.3d 1118, 1122-23 (8th Cir.1996) (plaintiff entitled to cost of two Mercedes as reward for coining slogan for insurance company).

In the present case, the Harrier Jet commercial did not direct that anyone who appeared at Pepsi headquarters with 7,000,000 Pepsi Points on the Fourth of July would receive a Harrier Jet. Instead, the commercial urged consumers to accumulate Pepsi Points and to refer to the Catalog to determine how they could redeem their Pepsi Points. The commercial sought a reciprocal promise, expressed through acceptance of, and compliance with, the terms of the Order Form. As noted previously, the Catalog contains no mention of the Harrier Jet. Plaintiff states that he "noted that the Harrier Jet was not among the items described in the catalog, but this did not affect [his] understanding of the offer." (Pl. Mem. at 4.) It should have.

... Carbolic Smoke Ball itself draws a distinction between the offer of reward in that case, and typical advertisements, which are merely offers to negotiate. As Lord Justice Bowen explains: “It is an offer to become liable to any one who … selects to make extravagant promises..." etc. (see). For the alleged offer in this case, at most, an advertisement to receive offers rather than an offer of reward, plaintiff cannot show that there was an offer made in the circumstances of this case.

```

Yes, we see that.

Now we need to select which of the four options was NOT mentioned. Let's analyze each:

Option A: "A reward advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the obligations mentioned in the advertisement."

This is basically stating the principle from Carbolic Smoke Ball: "If a person decides to make extravagant promises... etc." In explanation, the judge asserts that Carbolic Smoke Ball advertisement "constituted an offer to anyone who Plays the obligation." We need to see if the judge explicitly states that: "A reward advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the obligations mentioned in the advertisement." In the Carbolic Smoke Ball discussion, the judge quotes: "It is an offer to become liable to any one who performs the conditions." Hmm the judge states: "It is an offer to remain liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition." The judge states: "It is an offer to become liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition." Actually it states: "It is an offer to become liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition …".

Specifically, the judge wrote: "It is an offer to become liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition." This is essentially the same concept. The principle is "A reward advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the obligations mentioned." That is indeed implied: The advertisement qualifies as a unilateral offer. The judge did mention that. He also references Carbolic Smoke Ball and other reward cases. So Option A is present.

Option B: "As long as someone fulfills the content specified in the reward advertisement, the advertiser must fulfill their obligation." Did the judge mention that? Actually the judge said: "It is an offer to be liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition." Option C: "A reasonable and objective person would not consider PepsiCo's advertisement to be an offer." This is indeed the Court's reasoning: "The court finds that no objective person would have understood the commercial as an offer." So Option C is present.

Option D: "Reward advertisements that ask people to take specific actions are generally based on non-commercial reasons." Did the judge mention that? He said "Reward advertisements that ask people to take specific actions are generally based on non-commercial reasons." Let's see if that is stated.

In the Carbolic Smoke Ball section, the judge reads: "Reward advertisements that ask people to take specific actions are generally based on non-commercial reasons." Did we see that? That makes it a principle: The advertisement is a reward for a specific action. So Option D says: "Reward advertisements that ask people to take specific actions are generally based on non-commercial reasons." The judge indeed references this idea but may not phrase it exactly as "generally based on non-commercial reasons." But the judge textual it: "often for noncommercial reasons." So that is present. The judge also quotes "the reward advertisement is typically an offer with a certain 'noncommercial reason' to do something." I think Option D is present.

Check Option B: It says "As long as someone fulfills the content specified in the reward advertisement, the advertiser must fulfill their obligation." Did the judge say that? The judge said "It is an offer to become liable to any one who ... performs the condition." That suggests that if the condition is performed, the advertiser must honor all terms of the offer. Also, in the Carbolic Smoke Ball case, the court said: "the plaintiff was entitled to the reward." But did the judge mention "must fulfill their obligation" referencing the advertiser must fulfill contractual obligations? Let's inspect.

In fact, in the Carbolic Smoke Ball case, the judge states: "...the sitting advertisement ... the contract is formed once the plaintiff meets the condition." But I want to locate the case. The judge quotes from Carbolic. The judge previously wrote: "It is an offer to become liable to any one who, before it is retracted, performs the condition." Then later: "the plaintiff purchased the ball and used it as directed, but contracted influenza." Actually the case used Carbolic to say that the plaintiff was entitled to the reward. The judge used this to illustrate that the advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the condition. That basically implies that if a person performs the condition, the advertiser must pay. So it seems Option B was implied.

But we should check each option more precisely.

Option A: "A reward advertisement is an offer to anyone who performs the obligations mentioned in the advertisement."
